newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-HK's Tsang embraces multilateralism.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-HK's Tsang embraces multilateralism.

text.p: Hong Kong's participation in regional financial cooperation pacts must not conflict with its multilateral agreements, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Tuesday.

"We in Hong Kong have always believed in a multilateral system, so the BIS (Bank for International Settlements ) is the ideal place for dealing in issues of this kind," Tsang said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television on Tuesday.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority along with the central banks of China, India, South Korea and Singapore were invited to join the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in September.

The BIS, based in Basle, promotes cooperation among central banks, serves as a centre for monetary and economic research and provides financial services to assist central banks in the management of their external reserves.
"Whatever course we take must be a natural one that is comfortable to all concerned so there is not one BIS that has a superior relationship with all the Asian central banks," Tsang said.
"I'm hoping that this whole network system that Hong Kong favors will find favor with other central bankers," he said.

Several Asian countries, including Hong Kong, last year signed bilateral pacts on repurchasing U.S. dollar government securities from each other as a way of maintaining liquidity and currency stability in difficult times.

Hong Kong is also a member of a forum of central banks in the region called EMEAP, or the Executive Meetings of East Asia Pacific central banks. Other members are Australia, China, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, New Zealand, Thailand and the Philippines.

Australia has long supported the idea of an Asian central bank similar to the BIS to help protect the region from major attacks on the local currencies, but many of the other Asian countries have been non-commital.
Tsang said Asian countries should work together on linking individual securities clearing systems.
He dismissed bankers' observations that Hong Kong's clearing system, the Central Moneymarkets Unit, could become a clearing system for the region.
"The CMU is doing very well, but it is largely a clearing house for debt issued in Hong Kong and we have no interest in going beyond that," he said.
"Of course we are working on ways the CMU and other clearing systems can link together as part of a network," he said.
